s01.slug: INT. THE CHAPEL AT THE MERCY — NIGHT
body: At 9:02 p.m. on the night he is supposed to be crowned, Whitaker Ransome is hiding in a church.

He stands at the altar step of the Chapel at the Mercy with his tie undone and a can of Mercy Ranch Water sweating in his left hand. The can is his cousin Colt’s product — “made with San Isidro spring water,” $9.99 a four-pack, a cartoon longhorn in aviators on the side — and at the moment it is one part San Isidro spring water to two parts the flask in his breast pocket. In his right hand are three index cards gone soft at the corners from his thumb. Six hundred yards east, the Mercy Ball comes through the cedar walls as bass, a steel guitar, and now and then the whoop of a man who has paid twenty-five thousand dollars for a table and intends to be heard from it.

The chapel seats a hundred and twenty and tonight seats one. Only the pin lights over the altar are on; the back half of the room goes down into dark like the deep end of a pool. It smells of lemon oil, cedar and the ghost of last weekend’s lilies. In the pew rack nearest him a glossy brochure promises “A Hill Country Feeling, West Texas Soul” at thirty-eight thousand dollars a weekend, linens extra. Whit has always liked the brochure. It is the most honest document on the ranch.

He squares the cards and clears his throat. Greer’s notes run down the margin of card one in her small upright hand: gratitude, legacy, the next Texas, one self-deprecating line. Under that, underlined twice: NO MORE THAN ONE. It’s the closest thing to a love letter his wife has written him since the wedding, and he means that nicely.

“Thank you all for being here,” he tells the empty pews. “I know some of you drove in from Dallas, and I want you to know — we see your sacrifice.” He leaves room for the laugh. He leaves room for the gratitude, which Greer says must feel unrehearsed and which he has now rehearsed nine times. “A hundred years ago, my great-great-grandfather stood on this land and—” And what. Looked at it. Wanted it. Greer has written STEWARDSHIP beside that line and circled it, which means it isn’t optional.

Somewhere in the stewardship he notices where his feet are. This exact square of polished cedar, under this exact pin light, is where he stood in May of 2019 and married Greer Talmadge in front of three hundred people and a photographer from Texas Monthly. He was sweating then too. “Here’s the thing,” he tells a hundred and twenty empty seats. “Last time I stood up here, I promised to love and honor a Ransome institution for the rest of my life. And that one’s going great.” The seats take it under advisement.

His parents built the chapel in 2003 on the site of the old stock pens and put their names on a brass plaque by the door, as if God might otherwise lose track. His father comes out here sometimes, alone, and always sits in the back, like a man in a waiting room who doesn’t want his name called. Whit has never asked why. In his family you don’t ask a man why he sits where he sits. You just don’t sit there.

Card two. This is the good one. He lifts the can to the rafters. “And I just want to say — I have waited for this night longer than Dallas has waited for a Super Bowl.” He holds for the laugh. The chapel holds it with him, politely, the way you hold a door for someone who turns out to be going the other way. Out in the dark a horse whinnies. Best review he’s had all week.
From the back pew, from the dark, a woman’s voice says: “It’s better without the joke about the Cowboys.”

He nearly drops the can. Mercy Ranch Water slops over his knuckles onto the cedar, and Mercy Events LLC will bill somebody for that. He knows the voice before he finds the face, the way you know a song from two notes: low, unhurried, the Permian still under the vowels. Everybody in Texas knows that voice. Everybody has heard it say almost nothing at a party.

She’s in the last pew, where the pin lights give out. Paloma Pruett Ransome: twenty-five, his father’s wife of eleven months, the card girl from Odessa who took four hundred and twelve thousand dollars off Amon Ransome in one night in the back room of the Petroleum Club and married him nine weeks later. Bunny Ashworth calls her the Pigeon, and Fort Worth thinks that’s the funniest thing it has ever heard. Whit has stood near her at a dozen events — a christening, two funerals, the Stock Show, a Thanksgiving at which she ate pie and nothing else — and said “Hey there” to her at every one, in the voice he uses on donors’ wives and other people’s dogs. They have never had a conversation.

Black column dress, nothing on it. A turquoise cuff on one wrist; on the other, a man’s steel watch, too big, sliding to the bone when she moves. Her shoes — black satin, eleven hundred dollars, the kind that pinch at every one of them — are lined up side by side just inside the back door, heels to the wall, as if this were somebody’s house and she’d been raised right. She doesn’t get up. Something small and red walks over her knuckles, finger to finger, and back.

“How long have you been back there?” he says. “Who’s it for?” “Sorry?” “The toast.” The red thing stops on her middle knuckle. “Who are you saying it to? Because it isn’t them.” She tips her head east, toward the roar.

“Listen—” Whit says, which is what he says when he hasn’t decided what to say. He looks down at the cards. Card three is the one he hasn’t practiced. In his own handwriting it reads: Thank you, Dad, for — and then nothing, crossed out twice, as if the nothing had been wrong too. He has been trying to finish that sentence since August. He sets the card face down on the front pew, gently, as if it might finish itself while nobody’s watching, and turns to face his father’s wife.
“What are you doing out here?” “What are you?” It isn’t a dodge, exactly. She sounds as if she actually wants to know, which at the Mercy Ball counts as indecent exposure.

choices.text: Make it a joke. ‘I was told this room had great acoustics and no relatives.’
choices.ledger: You met your father’s wife in the chapel and made it a bit.
response: “Honestly? I was told this room had great acoustics and no relatives.” He points up at the rafters, then down the aisle at her. “Acoustics check out. I’ll have to take the rest up with management.”

She enjoys it. He can see her enjoy it: something loosens at one corner of her mouth, and the chip stops moving. Then, with exactly the same pleasure, she names it. “You’re doing the thing where you’re charming at me.” A small nod, the way a judge nods at a clean cut. “It’s very good. It’s like watching a man tap-dance in a house fire.”
He laughs, because she’s right, and because it has been years since anyone told him what he was doing instead of clapping for it.

choices.text: Tell her the truth. You’re hiding.
choices.ledger: You told Paloma you were hiding from your own party.
response: The acoustics line is right there. It’s a good one. Instead he hears himself say, “I’m hiding.” He lifts the cards an inch, as evidence. “From my own party. Which I think is a first, even for this family.”

She looks at him long enough that he starts to regret it. Then: “Okay.” She slides six inches down the back pew, away from the aisle, leaving room. From her, he suspects, that’s practically an embrace.
“Me too,” she says. “From a different party. Same tent.”

choices.text: ‘Mrs. Ransome.’ Button the jacket. Be the son.
choices.ledger: You called her Mrs. Ransome in an empty church.
response: He does up the button of his jacket, which is what Ransome men do instead of standing up straighter. “Mrs. Ransome.” He gives it the full Fort Worth: warm, correct, an inch of distance built in like a cattle guard.

“Mr. Ransome.” Exactly as cool, exactly as correct. She looks at the button, then at his loose tie, then at the button again. Then, not unkindly: “You can button it all the way. I’ve seen the rest of the family. It doesn’t help.”

s02.slug: INT. THE CHAPEL AT THE MERCY — CONTINUOUS

body.text: She plays, and she plays fast. He tells her the pews are original Ransome cedar; she says she assumed so, they creak like the family. He takes a small bow at the altar step and she calls him “Mr. Acoustics” — once, and then never again, as if a nickname were a chip she only bets one time. It’s been a while since anybody kept up with him. It has been longer since anybody got there first.

“What are you hiding from?” she asks. Then she does something nobody else at the Mercy Ball will do tonight: she waits for the answer. He gives her the short version — the toast, the tent, six hundred people who have paid to watch him be grateful — and she listens to all of it with her chin on her fist on the pew back, as if it were interesting. That unsettles him more than flirting would. He can flirt in his sleep. He has, at least twice.

She calls him Mr. Ransome. She calls him Mr. Ransome when he asks if the music is too loud back there, and Mr. Ransome when he offers her the can, and Mr. Ransome in a tone that makes the name sound like a coat she’s holding out for him to put on. He lasts three exchanges. “Paloma—” he says, and she lets the word sit there between them, his, not to be taken back, and he knows he has lost something small and fair.

body: He comes halfway down the aisle and stops at the sixth pew, where the light runs out, and sits sideways on it with his arm along the back, like a man at a ballgame. She stays where she is. “The acoustics are better up front,” he says. “I like it back here.” She doesn’t say why. He’s beginning to notice that she doesn’t say anything for free.

“So. The toast. Be honest, I’m told I can take it.” “It’s good,” she says. “It’s very good. Except the parts that are you.” “Which parts are me?” “The pauses. You stop after every line like you’re waiting for somebody to tell you it’s allowed.” She turns the chip. “I’ve sat across from a lot of men telling a table what they’re about to do. The ones who mean it don’t wait.”

“Why aren’t you out there?” It comes out more honestly than he meant it to. It’s her party too; she married it. “Everyone at this party has already decided what I am.” She says it with no self-pity at all, the way you’d give the weather. “It saves me so much time.” “They’re not all—” he starts, and stops, because Bunny Ashworth is out there, and Bunny is, in every way that counts, all.

“Twenty-five thousand dollars a table,” she says, “to teach rural children to read. And they’ve hollowed out the books to put cactus in them.” “Succulents,” Whit says. “Greer would want me to say succulents.” “Is there a difference?” “About forty dollars a pot.” He saw the mockups in April. A leather Moby-Dick with an echeveria planted where the whale used to be. Nobody on the committee said a word. Neither did he.

She looks past him toward the door, where the brass plaque catches a little of the pin light: THE CHAPEL AT THE MERCY · TO THE GLORY OF GOD AND IN THANKSGIVING FOR THIS LAND · AMON & LORNA RANSOME · MMIII. “Were you here when they built it?”

“I was, what — nine? Ten?” He squints, actually trying. “I remember cement trucks. A lot of cement trucks. Honestly, I don’t remember that year at all. It’s like a skipped track.” He shrugs. “Fourth grade. Rough year for everybody.”

She doesn’t laugh. She doesn’t do anything. The chip stops on her knuckle and stays there, and she goes so still that for a moment the only thing moving in the back of the chapel is the second hand on the too-big watch. Whit reads it the way anyone would: he’s lost her. Nobody wants to hear about a rich kid’s fourth grade. He doesn’t blame her. It bores him too.

To change the subject he nods at her hand. “What is that?” The chip starts moving again — index, middle, ring, little, and back — the way other people crack their knuckles. She holds it up to the light: red clay, worn pale at the rim, a derrick stamped in the center. “Petroleum Club. Five thousand.” A small pause. “Your father’s.” “He’s going to want that back.” “He’s had eleven months to ask.”

She closes it in her fist. “Let’s do something. One true thing for one true thing.” “Like truth or dare.” “No dares. Just the truth part. And not a fact.” The fist opens; the chip is gone, then back. “Facts are cheap. Everybody in your family has a thousand facts. I want a true thing.”

dossier.text: Turns a worn red clay poker chip over her knuckles — Petroleum Club, $5,000. Sits in the back pew. Wouldn’t come up the aisle.

choices.text: Tell her the true thing: you’re afraid he’ll pick you.
choices.ledger: You told Paloma you were afraid your father would choose you.
response: He means to tell her about the polo scar. He hears himself say, “I’m afraid he’ll pick me.” Then, because it’s out and lying there on the cedar between them: “Everybody thinks I’m scared he won’t. I’ve been scared he will since I was twelve. If he picks me, I have to be it. There’s no back door on that.”

She takes it seriously. She doesn’t tell him he’ll be wonderful, which is what Greer would say, or that he’s being a baby, which is what Hadley would say. She just takes it, the way you take something handed to you that turns out heavier than it looked.

“Okay,” she says. “Mine.” She looks at the altar, not at him. “I came in here because it’s the only quiet building on two hundred thousand acres. I stayed because you were bad at this.” The chip turns once. “I liked watching.”

His phone buzzes against his ribs. Greer: “Where are you. Your father is on at 9:30. You are on at 9:40. Agenda: smile.” No question marks. His wife doesn’t use them in writing. She says they read as need.

Paloma is already up and collecting her shoes, two fingers hooked through the heel straps. It’s 9:14. “Count to a hundred before you come out,” she says. “People talk.” “About what?” “Whatever’s cheapest.” And she goes out the back door barefoot into the dark, the shoes swinging from her hand, and the door eases shut behind her on its pneumatic arm, and he is alone in a church again with a can of spiked spring water and nobody to perform for.

choices.text: Give her a true thing that isn’t the true thing. The polo scar.
choices.ledger: You told Paloma how you got the scar. She asked for something else.
response: “True thing.” He touches the scar through his left eyebrow, the one a photographer once said made him look like a senator who’d been in a fight. “Deerfield, junior year. Polo. A kid from Greenwich named Tad took a full swing at the ball and got me instead. Eleven stitches. Tad still sends a Christmas card every year. It’s always a picture of a boat.” He has told it at forty dinners. It has never once failed.

“That’s a fact,” she says. “I asked for a true thing.” “It’s a very true fact.” “Okay.” She pays him in exactly the same coin, without any rancor at all. “I was born in Odessa.” “Everybody knows that.” She tilts her head. “See how it feels?”

His phone buzzes against his ribs. Greer: “Where are you. Your father is on at 9:30. You are on at 9:40. Agenda: smile.” No question marks. His wife doesn’t use them in writing. She says they read as need.

Paloma is already up and collecting her shoes, two fingers hooked through the heel straps. It’s 9:14. “Count to a hundred before you come out,” she says. “People talk.” “About what?” “Whatever’s cheapest.” And she goes out the back door barefoot into the dark, the shoes swinging from her hand, and the door eases shut behind her on its pneumatic arm, and he is alone in a church again with a can of spiked spring water and nobody to perform for.

choices.ledger: Paloma went first. You still owe her one true thing.
response: “Ladies first,” he says. “It’s the Texas way. Also I’d like to see how it’s done.”
“Okay.” No hesitation; she has been dealt worse. She looks straight at him and says it plainly, like turning a card face up: “I’m not here for your father’s money.”
He laughs. Anybody would; half of Fort Worth would pay to have been in the room for that one. She doesn’t laugh. She waits for him to finish, patiently, and when he has, she says, “Your turn.”

He opens his mouth, and his phone buzzes against his ribs. Greer: “Where are you. Your father is on at 9:30. You are on at 9:40. Agenda: smile.” No question marks. His wife doesn’t use them in writing. She says they read as need.

Paloma is already up and collecting her shoes, two fingers hooked through the heel straps. It’s 9:14. “You owe me,” she says. “I’m good for it.” “Nobody in your family is good for it.” At the door she looks back once. “Count to a hundred before you come out. People talk.” “About what?” “Whatever’s cheapest.” And she goes out barefoot into the dark, the shoes swinging from her hand, and the door eases shut on its pneumatic arm, and he’s alone in a church with a debt he can’t remember agreeing to.

s03.slug: EXT. THE SOUTH LAWN — THE MERCY BALL TENT — NIGHT
body: He counts to a hundred. He gets to sixty-one, which for a Ransome is a long time to do what a woman says, and at 9:17 he’s out the back door and walking east across six hundred yards of dark toward the light. At 9:20 he comes in through the west flap of the tent, re-tying his tie with one hand and re-assembling his face with the rest of him: eyebrows up a quarter-inch, shoulders down, the smile loaded and ready. It’s a face that photographs as trustworthy. It has never once let him down, which isn’t the same as his having earned it.

The Mercy Ball is a white sailcloth tent the size of a hangar, pitched on the south lawn between the House and the Italy, and inside it six hundred of the richest people between Fort Worth and El Paso are pretending to be at a barn dance. Outside, valets are parking Escalades in the hay stubble. This year’s theme is Boots & Bindings. The centerpieces are leather-bound classics hollowed out and planted with succulents — Anna Karenina with a jade plant, The Grapes of Wrath with a barrel cactus, which nobody on the committee found funny. An ice sculpture of the R-Bar-M brand, eight feet across, is melting from the M. Silver stock troughs of crushed ice and Mercy Ranch Water stand at every tent pole. The brisket flew in from Lockhart this afternoon on Mercy One along with its pitmaster, who is being photographed beside it like a groom. A Grammy-winning Western swing band from Austin plays “Faded Love” for people who have never faded at anything. On the forty-foot LED wall behind the stage, Colt — pearl snap open to the sternum, Stetson with a GoPro mount — is live to 2.1 million people. “We’re so back, Ranch Royalty,” Colt says, forty feet tall. “Shout-out to my cousin. Future king. Respectfully, bro.” And down the middle of it all, led slowly between the tables so donors can stand beside him, comes a gray gelding named Deacon, who belongs to the Agriculture Commissioner and has his own handler and his own nondisclosure agreement. “The horse tests at plus nine,” the Commissioner’s comms girl tells someone, not quietly enough.

Greer finds him in four seconds. She always does; he has a theory that she had him chipped, like a Labrador. Camel silk to the floor, a dark-blond blowout that has survived every wind West Texas has thrown at it, and the heirloom earrings she bought herself at an estate sale in River Oaks and lets people assume were her grandmother’s. She doesn’t ask where he was. Not yet. She takes his arm and talks into his shoulder at the volume of a woman saying something sweet.

“Agenda. One: Kilgore needs three minutes from you on rural water values. He doesn’t know what they are, so you’ll tell him. Two: Pete Ashworth bought a boat. Forty-eight feet. Say forty-eight like it’s a lot. Three: Soren Vale’s people want the heir in the photo line after the speech. That’s you. Smile like it’s you.” “Mm,” Whit says. “That’s mine,” she says. “Get your own.” Then she turns to face him, pulls loose his one-handed knot and ties his tie properly, fast and flat, in front of everyone: a half-Windsor with the dimple dead center. He loves her for it. Not simply, but really. It’s one of the things about her he would say under oath.

His mother is holding court near the bar for Wes Kilgore and a Dallas donor in a bolo tie that cost more than the donor’s first house. Chanel jacket over jeans, a cream cashmere wrap, enormous sunglasses pushed up into her silver chignon, and the cane she doesn’t need planted like a flag. “Whit was always the gentle one,” Lorna is telling the Commissioner. “He’d cry over a coyote.” Everybody laughs. Kilgore laughs a second too long and says, “Ma’am, I’m just a cowboy who took a wrong turn on the way to the rodeo and ended up in public service,” which has nothing to do with anything and which, Whit will learn, he says about every eleven minutes. Whit laughs too. It’s an old story. He has heard it every Christmas he can remember. His mother kisses him on both cheeks, smelling of Shalimar and sparkling water, and tells him she is eleven years sober and drinking it all in.

His phone: a photo from Ximena. June at the window of her room in the Italy, nightgown and pink boots, nose flattened to the glass, waiting for fireworks that are almost two hours away. The caption reads: “She says she is on duty.” He sends back a shark, which in his family means I love you, and so does the shark.

By the brisket, Soren Vale — founder of Halcyon Compute, guest of honor, the reason for the blue pipe on the stage — is wearing a Patagonia vest over his tuxedo shirt and Luccheses so new they squeak, explaining something to a rancher with both hands. The rancher has the expression of a man being told about his own cows.

Bunny Ashworth has a cluster of wives by the pecan pies, which flew in from Fredericksburg. She hums first — a bar of “Amazing Grace,” which with Bunny is the sound of a safety coming off — and then: “I’m not saying she’s a gold digger, sugar. I’m saying she brought her own shovel.” The wives make the sound of a flock settling. Whit follows their eyes across the tent, though he already knows where they’ll land.

Paloma is at the edge of the dance floor, alone, shoes back on as if they had never come off. Nobody is dancing near her. There’s a ring of empty parquet around her that is technically nobody’s fault. She’s turning the chip over her knuckles and watching the band the way you’d watch weather come in.

body.text: She doesn’t look at him. He’s grateful. He said something true in a church fifteen minutes ago and he can still feel it on him, like sun on the back of the neck, and he isn’t sure his face can be trusted with it yet.

He catches himself drafting it — the true thing he owes her — the way he drafts toasts: an opener, a turn, a button. Then he catches himself polishing the button, and stops, because he has a feeling she’d hear the polish from across the tent.
He watches her the way you watch the one person in a room you were rude to. She doesn’t look over. That’s fair. He keeps checking anyway.

body: At the far bar, under the string lights, his sister is talking low with Royce Teague. Hadley’s in a black tuxedo jumpsuit, a Patek on her wrist she would rather die than mention, her nails bitten to the quick. Teague is wearing aviators, at night, in a tent, and custom ostrich boots with his company’s ticker inlaid in turquoise up the shaft. He is not on the guest list. He is never on the guest list. He’s here anyway, the way weather is. Teague laughs at something, big and white-veneered. Hadley doesn’t. Whit notes it, files it under Hadley being Hadley, and lets the drawer close.

At 9:30 the band finishes a song and the lights over the head table come up, and his father’s chair is empty. It’s the tall chair, the only one at the table with arms. Amon Ransome has been on time for everything for seventy-six years, including, by family legend, his own birth. At cocktails he looked fine — six-four in a black tux and the silverbelly hat, receiving people by the ice brand like a bishop — though he kept his left hand in his pocket the whole hour, like a man guarding his wallet in Rome. Whit noticed the pocket. He decided it was a habit he’d never noticed. Greer looks at the chair, then at her watch, then at the chair. The band, sensing something, starts another song.

At 9:31, across the tent, a phone lights Paloma’s face from below. He watches her read it. Her face changes — not much; a door closing somewhere in a big house — and it is the only time tonight he will see it do that in public. She puts the phone away. She leaves by the east flap, toward the barns, not hurrying, which is how Whit knows she’s hurrying.

choices.text: Follow her. Casually. You’re extremely casual.
choices.ledger: You left the tent four seconds after your father’s wife.
response: Somewhere behind him Bunny’s humming stops. He doesn’t hear it stop; he only notices, later, that it isn’t there anymore. He’s out the east flap before he has decided to be, walking with the specific nonchalance of a man who would like six hundred people to know he’s just getting some air.

choices.ledger: You told Greer you were going to find your father.
response: He thumbs “Finding Dad” and is through the east flap before it delivers. Her reply lands in under three seconds: “Bring him in from the left. Cameras are right.” Then, a second bubble: “Thank you.” He stops in the dark grass to look at it. His wife almost never types that. She says it’s implied by the relationship.

choices.ledger: You asked your sister for help. She gave it.
response: He cuts across the parquet to the far bar. Teague sees him coming and peels off with a clap on the shoulder — “Brother” — and a gust of cologne like a cigar humidor that has been to church. Hadley doesn’t watch him go.

“Where’s Dad?” “He was gray at cocktails.” She says it low, into her bourbon. “Don’t tell him I said gray.” And for a second there she is: the girl who pulled calves at three in the morning and never complained to anyone who could hear. “Go. I’ll stall Soren. I’ll explain groundwater law to him until he cries.”

s04.slug: EXT. BEHIND THE CUTTING BARN — NIGHT
body: The cutting barn shows the party its good side. Floodlights wash the front of it white; horse trailers stand in a row with their ramps down; a cutting exhibition ended twenty minutes ago and a few hands are still walking horses out, and warm air breathes from the open aisle, where the floor is radiant-heated so the horses won’t get cold feet. The floor cost forty thousand dollars. Hadley once worked it out at Thanksgiving, out loud, per horse, per winter.

Around back there is none of that. The light stops at the corner of the barn like a property line. Behind it: a caliche service road, white under the stars; a pipe fence; black pasture running off to nowhere; a windmill clanking somewhere out in the dark on a wind Whit can’t feel. From the tent, faint as a radio in somebody else’s car, Colt’s livestream: “—so back—”
He finds Paloma by the white of her arms.

body.text: She doesn’t look up. “You followed me.” “I followed—” He stops, because he’s seen what she’s kneeling beside. “Him.” “Okay.”

body: His father is on the ground. Amon Ransome, six-four, seventy-six, chairman and chief executive, is down on one hip on the caliche with his legs out in front of him like a child’s. His silverbelly hat lies upside down in the dirt a yard away. The black tuxedo is white with dust all down one side, the side he fell on. His left hand is out of his pocket now, and it’s shaking — not a tremble, not a cold man’s shiver, but a steady, mechanical shake, like something left running. Whit has never seen his father’s hand do anything it wasn’t told to do.

And Amon is talking. It’s the voice — the boardroom voice, deep and slow and Old Testament, the one that has fired company presidents and farriers with the same calm. “You’re on my land,” he says. “I told you. I told you once.” He’s looking past both of them, at the fence line. Whit looks at the fence line. There is nobody at the fence line. There’s the pipe fence and the dark and the windmill turning. He looks again, harder, the way you look for a deer someone swears is right there. Nobody.

Maybe it’s the dust. The chalky, burnt-lime smell of caliche coming up off his father’s coat, and his father on the ground, and the dark. Something happens to Whit that he has no word for and no time for: a tightness under the ribs; the color of dusk, though it’s full night; a hard, flat sound in a small closed space. Then it passes, the way a cramp passes, and he’s a grown man in a tuxedo behind a barn.
Stroke, he thinks, and the word is so big he can’t pick it up.

Paloma is on her knees on the caliche in her black dress with one palm flat on his father’s chest and the other holding his good hand, and she’s talking to him low and steady, the way you’d talk to a horse caught in wire. “Ya, ya. Tranquilo. Aquí estoy.” Then English, same voice: “It’s me. You’re at the Ball. You came out for some air. There’s nobody there.” She doesn’t look frightened. She doesn’t look surprised. She looks like someone doing a thing she has done before, and Whit notices that the way you notice a step that isn’t where it should be — and steps over it.

body.text: His phone buzzes in his pocket. Then again. Greer, wanting the left side of the tent. He doesn’t look.
Hadley said gray, he thinks. Hadley was right. Hadley is always right; it’s her worst quality, and he’d give a great deal right now for her to have been wrong once.

She looks up at him. “Whit.” It’s the first time she has ever said his name — not Mr. Ransome, not anything — and it moves him more than anything else back here, which he will think about later and not enjoy. “I need help,” she says. “Nobody else. Now.”
body.else: She looks up at him and tells him what she needs in short words, the way you give directions to someone who is already driving. “Help. Nobody else. Now.”

body: “If anyone sees him like this,” she says, “it’s on Bunny’s Instagram by ten and on Bloomberg by Monday.” She isn’t being dramatic. She’s quoting odds.
On the far side of the wall, the horses stand on their forty-thousand-dollar floor. On this side, the king sits on bare caliche, which nobody ever thought to heat.

Amon’s eyes come off the fence line and find his son. For two long seconds nothing happens in them. Whit watches his father look at him the way you look at a man in an airport who might be someone you went to school with. One. Two. Then it lands — Whit sees the exact moment it lands — and right behind recognition comes shame, enormous, and right behind shame, faster than anything, the old contempt, pulled over it like a tarp over a wreck. “Don’t stand there,” Amon says, “like a heifer at a gate.”

dossier.text: You found him on the ground behind the cutting barn during the Ball, ordering someone off his land. There was nobody there.

choices.ledger: You and Paloma got your father inside without a soul seeing.
response: He gets down in the caliche — the knees of the tux go white at once; Greer will have views — hooks his father’s hat out of the dirt with two fingers, and gets an arm under his father’s shoulder. Paloma takes the other side without being asked. Amon is heavier than any man should be, heavier than his size, as if he were made of something denser than other people.
“On three,” Paloma says, and counts in Spanish, and on tres they get him up. They go the dark way, through the back of the barn, where nobody is.

choices.ledger: You called Tack. Of course you called Tack.
response: His phone is out before he has finished deciding. Tack is the third favorite in it, after Greer and June’s school. It rings once. “I’m coming around the back, Bud.” Engine noise. Gravel. Tack is already driving.
Already. Whit hasn’t told him where. He looks at Paloma. She’s combing the caliche out of his father’s white hair with her fingers, and she doesn’t explain.

choices.ledger: You knelt in the caliche and called him Dad.
response: He kneels in the caliche, right in front of his father, close enough to smell the dust and the bourbon and the bay rum. He doesn’t say anything clever. He doesn’t say anything but the one word. “Dad.”

Amon’s eyes come to him from somewhere a long way off. Then his good hand closes on Whit’s wrist, hard, harder than a man of seventy-six should be able to grip anything, and he says, quite clearly, not to the man in front of him: “Get in the truck, son. Stay in the truck.”

Then he’s back. Whit watches him come back. And he is furious — furious to be seen, furious at the hand on the wrist, which he lets go of as if it belonged to somebody else. There is no truck. Whit doesn’t know why the sentence has made his hands go cold.
He picks up the hat. He gets an arm under his father’s shoulder, and Paloma takes the other side, and on her count they get him up.

s05.slug: INT. THE HOUSE — THE OLD ROOM — NIGHT
body: They go the dark way: through the back door of the cutting barn and down the long aisle, past stalls where horses swing their heads around to watch three people in evening clothes walk like one badly assembled animal. The floor is warm. Whit can feel it through his shoes, and he can feel his father feel it through his boots — a small, surprised give in the old man’s weight, as if he’d forgotten what money could do. Out the north end. Across forty yards of lawn the party lights don’t reach. Into the mudroom of the House: the old House, the 1928 limestone one, the one the Italy was later built around like a stucco fist.

The hall smells of saddle soap and Pledge, exactly as it did when he was six. Paloma steers. She knows which boards creak — the third one past the linen closet, the long one at the turn — and without a word she moves the three of them around both. Whit grew up in this house. He didn’t know about either board.

At the turn of the hall, framed in barnwood, hangs the Texas Monthly cover from 1986: his father at thirty-six on a fence rail, a buzzard on the post behind him, under the headline THE VULTURE OF MIDLAND. Amon hung it himself, at eye level. When people ask about it, he says it’s the nicest thing anyone wrote about him that decade.

The old room is at the end. Whit has been inside it maybe five times in his life, always summoned. It’s smaller than he remembers, which is the rule with rooms, but it’s more than that: it’s narrow, a cell, really, for a man who owns two hundred and twelve thousand acres. A narrow iron bed, made tight enough to bounce a quarter. A saddle on a wooden stand, oiled. A King James Bible on the nightstand with a rubber band around it, as if it might otherwise get out. A hat hook by the door. A 1970s Zenith radio in wood grain, its dial glowing faint orange, tuned to nothing.

And on the nightstand beside the Bible, a baby monitor. White plastic, one small green light. The same model as June’s. Whit knows it’s the same model because Greer had June’s overnighted from Dallas after reading forty reviews aloud to him in bed. He looks at it. He decides not to think about it. He has been told he’s extremely good at that.

Paloma gets Amon onto the edge of the bed. She opens his collar, two studs, and drops them in her palm without looking. She runs water in the little bathroom and brings it back in a glass and holds it until his good hand takes it. She takes the hat from Whit — he didn’t know he was still holding it — and hangs it on the hook. All of it fast, unshowy, in order, like a pit crew.

And Amon puts himself back together in front of them. Whit watches it happen. It takes about four minutes. First the breathing slows. Then the shoulders come back. The left hand goes into the pocket of the tux and stays there. The eyes, which were somewhere else, come home and clear and narrow, and the face that has frightened three generations of Texas oilmen reassembles itself piece by piece, like a man buckling on armor in a hurry and getting every buckle. In four minutes he is nearly the lion again. Nearly. There’s still dust in his hair.

body.text: He won’t look at Whit at all. Not once, not even by accident. He looks at the saddle, the radio, the glass in his hand, the black window, anywhere else. Whit stands by the door with his arms at his sides and can still feel the grip on his wrist, a bracelet of pressure, as if his father had left something there and gone.

When he speaks, he says it to the window. “A man who needs to be liked,” Amon says, coldly and clearly, “will be owned by whoever likes him.” Whit has known his father for thirty-three years and can translate. It means thank you. It also means get out.
body.else: Then he looks at his son, steadily, the way he’d look at a horse he hasn’t made up his mind about. “A man who needs to be liked,” Amon says, coldly and clearly, “will be owned by whoever likes him.” Whit has known his father for thirty-three years and can translate. It means thank you. It also means get out.

body: Paloma walks him out. In the hall she pulls the door almost shut behind her — not all the way; she leaves a hand’s width, and Whit sees her glance once at the gap, measuring it — and they stand in the narrow hall under the Vulture of Midland, close, because the hall was built in 1928 for thinner people with less to say to each other.

Up close she smells of cedar and caliche. They both do. There is pale dust on the black of her dress and pale dust on his lapel, and she reaches up and brushes his lapel with two flat strokes of her hand, quick and practical, the way you’d knock the dust off a saddle — and then stops, her hand still raised, as if she has caught herself doing something in public. She puts the hand down.

body.text: “You said you were afraid he’d pick you,” she says. “You should see your face right now.” “What’s my face doing?” “It’s afraid he won’t.”

body: “Nobody,” she says, very quietly, because the door is open a hand’s width. “Not your wife. Not your sister. Nobody.” “Paloma—” “Not for me. For him.” She tips her head at the door. “He’s going to walk out there in twenty minutes and stand up in front of six hundred people, and he needs this to have never happened. Can you give him that?”

choices.ledger: You promised Paloma you’d tell no one about the barn.
response: “I promise,” he says. No joke on it. He finds he means it all the way down, which is not a place he goes often.

She looks at him for a long time — long enough that it becomes a little uncomfortable, then very uncomfortable, then something else — the way you’d check a man’s math before you let him carry your money. “Okay,” she says.
She believes him. He watches her decide to. And walking back out through the mudroom toward the noise, he finds he very much wants to be the kind of man who deserves it.

choices.text: ‘Scout’s honor.’ You were never a Scout.
choices.ledger: You promised Paloma, sort of. Scout’s honor.
response: He holds up three fingers. “Scout’s honor.” “You weren’t a Scout.” “I was asked to leave the Scouts.” “Why?” “Charm.”
Something happens in her face that is almost a laugh and gets swallowed before it reaches the hall. “Okay,” she says. “I’ll take sort of.”

choices.text: Ask her what’s wrong with him.
choices.ledger: You asked Paloma what’s wrong with your father. She didn’t answer.
response: “What’s wrong with him?” “He fell.” “That’s not an answer.” “It’s the one he’d give.”

She waits. She has, he’s noticing, an enormous capacity for waiting; it fills the hall the way water fills a stock tank. He doesn’t promise. He stands there in the dust and doesn’t, and he watches her notice that he doesn’t — and, oddly, the way she looks at him seems to go up a notch, not down.
“Go be charming,” she says. “Twenty minutes.”

s05b.slug: EXT./INT. TACK’S SILVERADO — THE BARN ROAD — NIGHT
body: Tack comes up the caliche with his headlights off. Whit hears the truck before he sees it — the particular ruined purr of a 2004 Silverado with six hundred thousand miles on it, which Tack won’t replace because “a new one asks questions” — and then it’s there, a darker shape on the white road, rolling the last thirty feet in neutral so it barely makes a sound.

Tack gets out. Sixty-seven, small and leathery, white mustache, reading glasses on a string around his neck. He’s wearing a pearl-snap shirt buttoned to the throat under a tuxedo jacket that doesn’t fit him across the shoulders. The jacket is rented. Odell Tackett has run a ranch with a twelve-car garage and a chandelier in the garage for thirty-five years, and he has never owned a tuxedo, and he never will. Every October he rents one from a place in Midland and returns it Monday with the receipt.

He doesn’t ask what happened. He crouches by Amon, says “All right, now” to nobody in particular, gets a shoulder under him and lifts — a man nearly a foot taller and fifty pounds heavier — into the cab of the truck in one smooth, unhurried motion, the way you’d load a bale you’ve loaded a thousand of. You don’t get a motion like that the first time. You get it by doing it before.

Tack and Paloma talk across Amon in short words, low, like two people who have worked the same night shift for months and quit using whole sentences. “I’ve got him, Mrs. Ransome.” “His collar.” “I know.” Tack opens the old man’s collar with two fingers. On the dash a Thermos of Folgers rolls when the door shuts and comes to rest against the windshield.

body.text: Tack looks at Whit. Then at Paloma. Then back at Whit, over the glasses, for a while. “Well,” he says. That’s all.

body: Then he turns to Whit, mild as milk. “Go on back to your party, Bud. Your daddy took a turn on the gravel. That’s all this was.”

It’s a perfect sentence. It’s so finished — no edges, nothing to grab — that it sounds less like something Tack just thought of than like a press release that has been sitting in a drawer a long time, waiting for the right night.

Paloma climbs into the cab beside his father and pulls the door to. Through the open window she holds out her hand, and Whit realizes he’s holding his father’s hat. He must have picked it up out of the dirt; he doesn’t remember doing it. The engine idles. The windmill clanks. Tack puts the truck in gear and keeps his boot on the brake, waiting, the way he has always waited for Whit — patient as a fence post — to finish doing whatever Whit is going to do.

dossier.text: Drives a 2004 Silverado with 600,000 miles because ‘a new one asks questions.’ Was already on his way to the barn when you called.

choices.text: Go back. Tack’s got it. Tack’s always got it.
choices.ledger: You let Tack handle it. He said that’s all it was.
response: He hands the hat through the window. Paloma sets it on her knees, crown down, the way you’re supposed to.
“Good man,” Tack says, and lifts two fingers off the wheel, and the truck rolls away up the road toward the House with its lights still off, a dark thing moving on a white road.
Whit stands behind the barn and hates how good it felt to be called that. For leaving. Best review he’s had all night.

choices.text: Climb in the bed of the truck. In the tux.
choices.ledger: You rode to the House in the bed of Tack’s truck, in your tuxedo.
response: He doesn’t hand over the hat. He puts a hand on the tailgate and goes over it into the bed of the truck, in the tux, and lands on a coil of baling wire and a sack of mineral lick. Tack looks at him in the rearview mirror for a long moment. Then he lets off the brake.

Two hundred yards of caliche at five miles an hour: Whit on his knees in the truck bed, holding the rail with one hand and his father’s hat with the other, the dust coming up white around him as if he’s being sifted.

At the House, Tack and Paloma get Amon out between them, and Paloma lets Whit carry the hat in through the mudroom and down the hall, past the Texas Monthly cover from 1986 — his father at thirty-six on a fence rail, under THE VULTURE OF MIDLAND — as far as the door at the end, and no further. There she takes the hat out of his hands.
“Twenty minutes,” she says. “Go be charming.” The door closes, gently, on his face.

choices.text: Ask Tack how many times he’s done this.
choices.cue: Tack said nothing. He usually doesn’t.
choices.ledger: You asked Tack how many times he’s done this.
response: He hands the hat through the window. Then, before he can talk himself out of it: “Tack. How many times have you done this?”
Tack looks at him over the reading glasses. It is a long look, perfectly friendly, the look of a man who has outwaited droughts. “Done what, Bud?”
Whit doesn’t have a word for what. Tack waits to see whether he’ll find one. He doesn’t. “Well,” says Tack, and lets off the brake.

As the truck slides past, Paloma looks at Whit through the open window — one look, quick — and he reads it as good question. He may be wrong. Then the truck is a dark shape going up a white road, and he’s alone with the windmill.
